analysis.one_liner: Repeals Dodd-Frank oversight of major payment and clearing systems, ending their too-big-to-fail designations.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the repeal on a party-line 33-25 vote, but the bill was reported to the calendar on the second-to-last day of Congress and never received a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Dodd-Frank lets a council of regulators label financial market utilities — the payment, clearing, and settlement systems that move money between banks and brokers — as 'systemically important,' which exposes them to extra regulation. This bill would erase that authority entirely, wiping out the whole section of Dodd-Frank that covers those systems. The House Financial Services Committee approved it, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Financial market utilities — clearinghouses, payment processors, and settlement systems, along with the banks and trading firms that depend on them — would escape designation as systemically important and the additional regulatory restrictions that come with it, avoiding compliance costs. Ordinary people get nothing in return; they simply carry more of the risk if one of these systems fails.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals title VIII of Dodd-Frank, eliminating the Financial Stability Oversight Council's power to designate financial market utilities — payment, clearing, and settlement systems — as systemically important [S2].
Entities designated as systemically important are subject to additional regulatory restrictions; repealing the designation authority removes that entire layer of oversight [S2].
The repeal restores the law as if title VIII had never been enacted, wiping out all of its regulatory provisions at once [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the residual risk. If a major payment or clearing system fails during a crisis and there is no federal framework for handling it, the disruption can freeze credit and payroll, and taxpayers can end up backstopping the fallout the way they did in 2008.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through added financial-stability risk

drawbacks.text: Removing the designation authority leaves no federal mechanism for identifying and regulating market utilities whose failure could spread through the economy, so risk would fall back on the public during a crisis [S2].

The good-faith objection: clearinghouses and payment systems already answer to other regulators (such as the SEC, CFTC, and Federal Reserve), so supporters argued the FSOC designation layer was duplicative and added cost without adding safety. An honest assessment is that repealing the whole title removes a backstop without a clear replacement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to a narrow set of financial firms in the form of avoided regulatory costs. The cost — higher systemic risk if a major clearing or payment system fails — is spread across everyone who depends on the financial system working in a crisis. The scale is lopsided: modest, certain savings for the industry against a low-probability but severe public risk.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it, but it sat on the House calendar and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Budd introduced the bill on November 3, 2017, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S1].
The committee held a markup on November 15, 2017, and voted 33-25 to order the bill reported [S5].

The committee did not formally report the bill until January 2, 2019 — more than 13 months after the markup and one day before the 115th Congress ended — when it was placed on the Union Calendar [S5].
The House never voted on the bill, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died without a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, Dodd-Frank's oversight of systemically important payment and clearing systems stayed in place, and the public kept that protection. The financial utilities that would have escaped designation did not get the relief they wanted — though the bill's passage through committee showed where a future attempt would start.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee Republicans
for.role: Majority bloc on the House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Voted with the committee majority (33-25) to order the bill reported out of committee

against.name: House Financial Services Committee Democrats
against.role: Minority bloc on the House Financial Services Committee

sides.party_line_note: The 33-25 committee vote split on party lines, with committee Republicans voting to report the bill and committee Democrats voting no; the bill drew zero cosponsors [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Financial market utilities (clearinghouses, payment and settlement systems)
industries.note: The bill would free these firms from being designated systemically important, removing extra regulation and compliance costs. The public's cost is the lost federal framework for managing their failure in a crisis.

industries.industry: Large banks and trading firms that rely on central clearing and settlement
industries.note: These firms' counterparties and infrastructure would face less oversight, lowering industry compliance costs. The risk of a settlement failure would shift toward the broader economy and potentially taxpayers.
